1303.title: A match
1303.hook: matchmaking is common in traditional communities
1303.howItsDone: In many traditional Jewish communities, a match is suggested by a matchmaker (shadchan), a teacher or a family friend; the families make inquiries, the two people meet, and the couple decides whether to go forward.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was confirmed: a second yes, chosen once you know more. Today a new stretch of the life cycle begins, before a couple has even met.

A Roman noblewoman, the midrash says, once put a sharp question to Rabbi Yose. If your God finished making the world, what has he been doing since? Matching couples, said Rabbi Yose. She laughed. She could do that herself; she had plenty of servants. In a single night she paired them all off. By morning they came to her bruised and complaining, each one wanting out. She went back to Rabbi Yose and admitted it. He told her that to God, joining two people is as hard as splitting the sea.
screen: `WHAT HAS GOD DONE SINCE?` → `MATCHING COUPLES.` → `ONE NIGHT, AND A BAD MORNING.`

segments.voice: You met Abraham's servant at the well back in your first year. Today, what he was doing there has a name. A shidduch is a suggested pairing, and the person who suggests it is a shadchan, a matchmaker. In traditional communities a match often begins this way: a shadchan, a teacher, a family friend says, I know someone. The two families ask questions. The two people meet. The Torah has its own matchmaking story. Abraham sends his servant to his homeland to find a wife for Isaac. At the well the servant asks God for a sign. Not beauty, not wealth: the young woman who, when he asks for a drink, gives it and offers to water his camels too. Before he has finished speaking, Rebekah comes out and does exactly that. He was looking for kindness that does more than it's asked. But a match is a suggestion, not an order. When the servant wants to leave with Rebekah, her family says they will call her and ask her. Her answer, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, is short: "I will go." Jewish law insists that a marriage needs both people's consent, and the rabbis read this moment as part of that teaching. Which brings us back to the noblewoman. She treated matching as sorting, done by morning. Rabbi Yose's answer says the opposite: a good match takes patience, knowledge of both people, and humility. The matchmaker only opens a door. The two people walk through it, or don't.
screen: `A MATCHMAKER SAYS: I KNOW SOMEONE.` · `A SIGN AT THE WELL: KINDNESS.` · `REBEKAH IS ASKED, AND ANSWERS.` · `NOT SORTING, BUT CARE.` · then, large: `A MATCH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind two people you know who don't know each other but should, and not only for romance: two new parents, two people who love the same odd hobby, a newcomer and a neighbor. Notice what each might bring the other, and how you'd make the introduction and then leave the next step to them, the way Rebekah's family left the answer to her.
Shidduch: a match. An introduction made with care by someone who knows both sides, and a yes that belongs to the two people. Today's word.
Your line: a match. As hard as splitting the sea, and worth the care. That's today, done.

1304.title: Engagement
1304.howItsDone: In many Ashkenazi communities, a tena'im (engagement agreement) is read and signed, often on the wedding day before the ceremony, and the mothers of the couple break a plate together.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shidduch, and your line was a match: an introduction made with care, the yes left to the two. Today the match turns into a plan.

A plain china plate, wrapped in a cloth napkin. Two women, the mothers of the bride and the groom, each take an edge. A few minutes earlier, a short document was read aloud and signed in this room. Now, at a signal, they bring the plate down hard on the back of a chair. It shatters inside the napkin. People clap and call out mazel tov. At some Ashkenazi weddings, this happens shortly before the ceremony. The document is today's word, and the broken plate is its exclamation mark.
screen: `A PLATE IN A NAPKIN.` → `TWO MOTHERS, ONE SIGNAL.` → `IT SHATTERS. MAZEL TOV.`

segments.voice: Tena'im means conditions. It's an engagement agreement, setting down in writing what the two sides have agreed: that there will be a wedding, and what each family will bring to it. In earlier generations it could be signed long before the wedding. Today, couples who keep the custom often sign it on the wedding day itself, in a side room before the ceremony. Why agree at all? The prophet Amos asks a question that sounds written for an engagement: "Can two walk together, except they be agreed?" A marriage is two people on a long road, side by side. The tena'im says, before the walking starts: here is what we have agreed, out loud, in front of others. And the plate? Explanations differ, and families keep the custom without settling them. Some say it's a warning: a broken engagement, like a broken plate, can't be glued back, so treat this promise seriously. Others hear the same note as the glass broken under the canopy, a memory inside joy, which comes in a few days. Some couples now write tena'im in their own words, about how they hope to share a home, make decisions, disagree, and keep learning. The old idea holds. Conditions aren't a sign of distrust. They're how two people say plainly what they are building, before they build it.

Tena'im: conditions. The engagement agreement, read and signed, and at some weddings sealed with a broken plate. Today's word.
Your line: conditions. Agreeing out loud is a way of caring, not of doubting. Until tomorrow.

1305.title: The canopy
1305.hook: the wedding canopy is a new home, open on every side like Abraham's tent
1305.carry: a house open on all sides
1305.howItsDone: A Jewish wedding takes place under a chuppah, a canopy of cloth on poles, sometimes a prayer shawl, sometimes held by friends; the couple stands beneath it as their first shared home.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tena'im, and your line was conditions: terms said out loud before the building starts. Today, the building itself, and it has no walls.

A pole at each corner. A cloth across the top. That's all. No walls, no door, no lock. Sometimes the cloth is a prayer shawl that belonged to a grandparent; sometimes it's embroidered, plain white, or a quilt friends stitched together. At some weddings, friends hold the poles by hand, and you can see their arms get tired. The couple walks in, and the wind comes straight through. This little shelter is where a Jewish wedding happens. Why would a wedding happen in a room you can't close?
screen: `A POLE AT EACH CORNER, ONE CLOTH.` → `NO WALLS, NO DOOR.` → `WHY A ROOM YOU CAN'T CLOSE?`

segments.voice: Start with the word. In Psalm nineteen, the sun rises like a groom. The King James puts it: "as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber." The Hebrew for that chamber is a form of chuppah. In the Bible it's a wedding room; at a Jewish wedding it has shrunk to a cloth on poles, and kept its meaning. The couple stands under it together, and tradition treats the chuppah as their first shared home, before there's a lease or a key. Being brought under it is part of what makes them married. Now the open sides. You met Abraham at his tent back in your first year, sitting "in the tent door in the heat of the day," then running to meet strangers with water for their feet and bread. The midrash adds a detail the verse doesn't: his tent had openings on every side, so travelers from any direction found a door facing them. The chuppah, some teachers say, carries that tent into every wedding. A Jewish home is meant to be open to guests from its very first minute. And what holds it up? Only cloth; a gust can lift it. When friends hold the poles, the picture is plain: a new home stands because the people around it keep it standing. A house open on all sides needs, and welcomes, everyone nearby.

Let your home come to mind as it is right now, and ask: if every side had a door, who would walk in, and who could, if you opened one more side? Let one name come, and hold it gently.
Chuppah: the wedding canopy. A first home, with a roof and no walls, open like Abraham's tent. Today's word.
Your line: a house open on all sides. The door faces every direction. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1306.title: The ketubah read
1306.hook: the marriage contract is read aloud under the chuppah
1306.howItsDone: Before a Jewish wedding, witnesses sign the ketubah, the marriage contract; under the chuppah it is read aloud, traditionally in Aramaic, often followed by a translation, and some couples later display it at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was chuppah, and your line was a house open on all sides. Today, under that open roof, someone unfolds a document and starts to read.

Under the canopy, the music has stopped. The couple stands close. Someone steps forward with a large sheet of paper, sometimes plain, sometimes painted with flowers, birds, a border of Hebrew letters, and reads aloud, in Aramaic. Some guests follow every word; some only hear the rhythm. At some weddings a translation comes after. It isn't a poem. It's a contract, with obligations and a sum of money in it. Why stop a wedding, at the moment everyone is waiting for, to read out a legal document?
screen: `THE MUSIC STOPS.` → `A DOCUMENT, READ IN ARAMAIC.` → `A CONTRACT, AT A WEDDING?`

segments.voice: Ketubah means, simply, the written thing. It's the marriage contract, and it sets out what the husband owes his wife. Where do those duties come from? In Exodus, in a law about a man who takes a second wife, the Torah lists what he may not hold back from the first. In the King James wording: "her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage, shall he not diminish." Food, clothing, and closeness. The rabbis read that verse as a floor, not a ceiling: the least a marriage owes, written down so no one can pretend it was never said. The ketubah also promises the wife a sum of money if the marriage ends, by divorce or by her husband's death. The Talmud gives the reason: so a husband couldn't send his wife away lightly. In a world where a woman could be left with nothing, the rabbis put a cost on leaving and her name on the page. Why aloud? The ketubah is signed by witnesses before the ceremony, then read in front of everyone, and a promise read out in a crowd is one the crowd can remember. Some hang their ketubah on a wall at home. Some couples today choose one with promises from both sides, in words they've thought through together. Either way, love is the reason. The writing is how it gets kept.
screen: `THE WRITTEN THING.` · `FOOD, CLOTHING, AND CLOSENESS.` · `A COST ON LEAVING.` · `READ IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.` · then, large: `PROMISED IN WRITING.`

If you're somewhere you can, say it quietly out loud, as if it were read under a canopy, and notice how it sounds outside your own head.
The ketubah read: the marriage contract, signed by witnesses and read aloud under the chuppah, so the promise is heard as well as written. Today's word.
Your line: promised in writing. Love makes the promise; the ink helps it last. Tomorrow, the singing.

1307.title: Seven blessings
1307.hook: seven blessings sung for the couple
1307.howItsDone: Under the chuppah, seven blessings (sheva brachot) are said or sung over a cup of wine, often by honored guests; in many communities they are said again at festive meals for the couple in the days after the wedding.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was promised in writing: the ketubah, read aloud under the canopy. After the contract comes the singing.

"The voice of joy, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride." The prophet Jeremiah spoke those words about Jerusalem in a bad season, when people said its streets would be empty, with no one left in them. He promised these sounds would be heard there again: laughter, and weddings. His words are still sung today, under a cloth on poles, over a cup of wine, for two people standing close. They sit at the very end of today's word.
screen: `THE VOICE OF THE BRIDE.` → `PROMISED TO EMPTY STREETS.` → `SUNG UNDER THE CANOPY.`

segments.voice: Under the chuppah, over a cup of wine, seven blessings are said or sung for the couple. The Talmud lists them. Often, different guests are honored with one blessing each: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend. The blessings start wide: the wine, then God who created everything for his glory, and who formed the human being. Then they move closer, to Zion rejoicing in her children coming home. Then closer still, to this couple, called loving companions, asking that they be gladdened as God gladdened the first human in the garden of Eden. A wedding, here, is set inside the story of creation. The last blessing piles up words for happiness, one after another, then borrows Jeremiah's promise: in the streets of Jerusalem there will again be heard the voice of the groom and the voice of the bride. One couple's joy is tied to a city's hope. And the blessings keep going. In traditional communities, in the days after the wedding, friends host festive meals for the couple, and the blessings are said again at the table. Those meals are called sheva brachot too. Tradition looks for a new face at each one, a guest who wasn't at the earlier celebrations, so the joy is new for someone. Seven blessings aren't a single moment. They're a circle that keeps widening.
screen: `SEVEN BLESSINGS OVER WINE.` · `FROM CREATION TO THE COUPLE.` · `THE VOICE OF THE GROOM AND BRIDE.` · `A NEW FACE AT EVERY TABLE.` · then, large: `SEVEN BLESSINGS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind two people who share a life, newlyweds, grandparents, old friends, and picture them at their own table. Wish them joy quietly, with no advice and no conditions. If you pray, hold them inside Jeremiah's words, the voice of joy and the voice of gladness; if not, let the wish itself be enough.
Sheva brachot: seven blessings, sung under the chuppah and again at the meals after, from creation to the couple. Today's word.
Your line: seven blessings. Joy grows each time someone new comes to share it. Until tomorrow.

1308.title: Breaking the glass
1308.hook: a glass is broken to remember Jerusalem, even in joy
1308.howItsDone: At the end of a Jewish wedding ceremony, a glass wrapped in cloth is broken underfoot, traditionally by the groom and at some weddings by both partners, as a remembrance of Jerusalem's destruction; the guests then shout mazel tov.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sheva brachot, ending with the voices of groom and bride in Jerusalem's streets. Today, that same Jerusalem, remembered with a crash.

A wedding feast in Babylonia, in the days of the Talmud. A rabbi named Mar, the son of Ravina, is marrying off his son. The guests are rabbis, and they're getting very merry. Louder, and louder. So Mar brings out a precious cup, an expensive one, and breaks it right in front of them. The room changes. The Talmud says they became serious. Something shifted in the middle of the joy, and that shift is today's custom.
screen: `A FEAST IN BABYLONIA.` → `THE RABBIS GET MERRY.` → `A COSTLY CUP, SHATTERED.`

segments.voice: At the end of a Jewish wedding ceremony, a glass wrapped in cloth is set on the ground. The groom brings his foot down on it, and at some weddings both partners do. A crunch, then the whole room shouts mazel tov, and the music starts. Tradition ties the broken glass to the destruction of Jerusalem and its Temple. There's a Hebrew phrase for customs like this: zecher l'churban, a remembrance of the destruction. Psalm one hundred thirty-seven speaks in the voice of exiles by the rivers of Babylon. In the King James words: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." A verse later, the speaker vows to set Jerusalem "above my chief joy." A wedding is a chief joy, so at that moment Jerusalem is set above it. In some communities those verses are said just before the glass is broken. Mar's cup, though, wasn't mourning a city. He was keeping a party from forgetting itself. Later tradition joined the two ideas, and the custom holds both. The glass doesn't cancel the joy: mazel tov comes right after the crash, not instead of it. A happy couple and a loss still remembered share one room. Some add one more meaning: love, like glass, is precious and can break, so handle it with care.
screen: `A GLASS UNDER A FOOT.` · `A REMEMBRANCE OF THE DESTRUCTION.` · `MAR'S CUP AT THE FEAST.` · `THE CRASH, THEN MAZEL TOV.` · then, large: `JOY AND MEMORY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something good, coming soon or just past, and let one person or place you've lost come to stand beside it, someone who would have been glad to be there. Hold both at once, without choosing between them or rushing either: let the joy stay joy, and the memory stay memory.
Breaking the glass: a remembrance of Jerusalem at the height of a wedding, and then the shout of mazel tov. Today's word.
Your line: joy and memory. One room is big enough for both of them. See you tomorrow.

1309.title: The first moment
1309.hook: the couple spends a few minutes alone right after the ceremony
1309.howItsDone: Right after a traditional Jewish wedding ceremony, the couple spends a few minutes alone in a private room (yichud), often breaking a wedding-day fast together, while friends stand by the door as witnesses.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was joy and memory: the crash of the glass, then mazel tov. Today, right after the shouting, the couple slips away down the hall.

A small side room, down the hall from the party. A table, two chairs, a little food. The door closes, and a couple of friends stand outside it so nobody knocks. Inside are two people married a few minutes ago, alone together for the first time all day. Down the hall the band is tuning up, the photographer is checking the light, the guests are finding their tables. For a short while, nobody can reach the two of them. The room has a name, and so do these minutes.
screen: `A SMALL ROOM DOWN THE HALL.` → `FRIENDS AT THE DOOR.` → `NOBODY CAN REACH THEM.`

segments.voice: Yichud means being alone together, and it belongs to the wedding; it isn't a break from it. Some authorities count these minutes alone, as a married couple, as part of the wedding itself. The friends at the door serve as witnesses that the two were alone together. Then there's the meal. In some communities the bride and groom fast on their wedding day until the ceremony. The food in that room is where they break the fast side by side, the first meal of their marriage, with no one else at the table. Behind it is a law in Deuteronomy. A new husband isn't sent out to war or loaded with public duties. In the King James words, "he shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer up his wife which he hath taken." The Torah treats the start of a marriage as something the world should leave alone for a while. Yichud is that idea in miniature: a few minutes the whole day agrees not to touch. Before the speeches and photos, before anyone else takes a piece of the day, there's a moment that belongs only to the two of them. Whatever they say in there, or don't, is theirs. Then the door opens, and they walk out to the music. A shared life needs a little protected quiet at its start, and the people who love them keep watch at the door.
screen: `PART OF THE WEDDING ITSELF.` · `THE FIRST MEAL, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `FREE AT HOME, THE TORAH SAYS.` · `A MOMENT THAT'S ONLY THEIRS.` · then, large: `THE FIRST MOMENT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who rarely gets a moment to themselves, a parent of small children, a caregiver, a friend always on call, and picture one small way you could stand at their door: a task taken off their hands, the noise kept down. If you're the one who never gets quiet, let these minutes be yours, and let nobody knock.
Yichud: alone together, right after the ceremony. And a week closes: a match, conditions, the canopy, the ketubah read, seven blessings, the glass, and the first moment. Today's word.
Your line: the first moment. Some quiet is worth guarding. A week done, and a wedding with it.
